title: Immune control of lethal Nipah virus infection: the critical role of host macrophages

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand the role of different immune cell populations in controlling Nipah virus (NiV) infection, given the poor understanding of the immunopathogenesis of this highly pathogenic zoonotic virus.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used wild type mice and CD169-DTR transgenic mice to investigate the role of various immune cell populations in NiV infection, with African green monkeys serving as a model for severe human Nipah disease.
analysis.methods: The researchers analyzed the role of T lymphocytes, B lymphocytes, NK cells, and macrophages in NiV infection using depletion experiments and transgenic mice.
analysis.main_results: T lymphocytes were found to play a critical role in controlling NiV infection, while B lymphocytes and NK cells were not essential. Depletion of phagocytes, specifically CD169 + macrophages, increased susceptibility to NiV infection.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study highlights the critical role of CD169 + macrophages in controlling NiV infection, which may help in understanding the immunopathogenesis of this highly lethal disease.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that targeting CD169 + macrophages could be a potential therapeutic strategy for NiV infection, and may aid in the development of better diagnostic tools and preventive measures.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the use of mice as a model, which may not fully represent human disease. The findings in mice need to be validated in human studies.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the role of various immune cell populations in controlling Nipah virus infection using mice and transgenic models. It demonstrated the critical role of T lymphocytes and the importance of CD169 + macrophages in controlling NiV infection, highlighting potential therapeutic and diagnostic strategies.

title: Deterministic–stochastic fractional-order modeling and optimal control of Nipah virus in hypertensive nephrosclerosis

analysis.research_question_and_background: Nipah virus is a zoonotic virus that causes severe respiratory and neurological disease and is spread through pigs, bats or contaminated food.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This research develops a fractional-order mathematical model to investigate the co-infection dynamics of hypertensive nephrosclerosis and Nipah virus infection.
analysis.methods: The model is kept positive and bounded to guarantee biological reality, and the disease-free equilibrium E p l is studied.
analysis.main_results: The basic reproduction number R 0 l p < 1 implies extinction of the infection while R 0 l p > 1 implies small outbreaks developing into epidemics.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These results are backed up by bifurcation analysis, global stability analysis and existence and uniqueness proofs for the solution.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Real Malaysian co-infection data was used to parameterise the model, and simulations were carried out for both deterministic and stochastic fractional systems.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The fractional-order parameter has significant impact on the infection rates and convergence behaviour.

analysis.summary_en: This study develops a fractional-order mathematical model to investigate the co-infection dynamics of hypertensive nephrosclerosis and Nipah virus infection. The model is designed to be biologically realistic and ensures positivity and boundedness. The basic reproduction number R0lp determines whether the infection will go extinct or lead to epidemics. The results are supported by bifurcation analysis, global stability analysis, and existence and uniqueness proofs. The model is parameterized using real Malaysian co-infection data and simulations are conducted for both deterministic and stochastic systems. The study provides insights into the interaction between hypertensive nephrosclerosis and Nipah virus transmission, supporting the design of effective and economically feasible control strategies.

title: Competitive inhibition of the Nipah virus matrix protein by conivaptan: from binding pocket dynamics to protein–membrane interactions

analysis.research_question_and_background: The recurrent outbreaks of Nipah virus since its first emergence have intensified efforts to identify effective antiviral therapeutics.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The matrix protein is a key structural protein that maintains virion architecture and plays a crucial role in anchoring the virus to the host plasma membrane.
analysis.methods: Binding of phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) to the matrix protein promotes conformational changes that facilitate membrane association and initiate viral assembly.
analysis.main_results: Using virtual screening of FDA-approved drugs combined with ensemble docking, we identified conivaptan as a potential inhibitor of the Nipah virus matrix protein.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The multivalent interactions of conivaptan establish stable binding within the PIP2-binding pocket while simultaneously rewiring protein-membrane interactions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Together, these findings identify conivaptan as a promising repurposable inhibitor of the Nipah virus matrix protein and provide a mechanistic framework for targeting virus-membrane interactions during viral assembly.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: In the presence of PIP2, NiVM anchors to the membrane through multiple charged residues, resulting in pronounced local bilayer deformation, an early signature of membrane remodeling.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to identify effective antiviral therapeutics for Nipah virus, which has caused recurrent outbreaks. The research focused on the matrix protein, a key structural component involved in viral assembly and membrane association. The study used virtual screening and ensemble docking to identify conivaptan as a potential inhibitor of the Nipah virus matrix protein. The findings suggest that conivaptan competes with PIP2 for binding to the matrix protein and disrupts its interaction with the host membrane, thereby suppressing membrane deformation. These results provide a mechanistic framework for targeting virus-membrane interactions during viral assembly. The study's evidence is based on computational methods, which may have limitations in directly translating to biological systems. However, the findings offer a promising avenue for repurposing conivaptan as an antiviral agent against Nipah virus.

title: Vertical Transmission of Nipah Virus in an Experimentally Infected Nonhuman Primate: A Brief Report and Description of Histopathological Lesions.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Nipah virus (NiV) is a highly pathogenic henipavirus that causes severe, often fatal disease in humans and animals.
analysis.study_design_and_population: African green monkeys have been used extensively to investigate NiV disease and are the only nonhuman primate model that accurately recapitulates human NiV pathogenesis.
analysis.methods: Here, we describe histopathological lesions in the reproductive tissues of an incidentally pregnant female African green monkey that succumbed to NiV disease.
analysis.main_results: We employed multiplex immunohistochemistry techniques to profile specific cell populations that identified NiV antigen in both maternal and fetal cells of the placenta, which has not been previously described in nonhuman primate models of NiV disease.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings provide novel insights into the vertical transmission of NiV in nonhuman primate models, highlighting the potential for placental transmission.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results contribute to understanding the mechanisms of NiV transmission and may inform future studies on the virus's behavior in pregnant hosts.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a single incidentally pregnant female African green monkey, which may affect generalizability, and the evidence is based on histopathological analysis with no statistical analysis provided.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the vertical transmission of Nipah virus in an experimentally infected nonhuman primate, specifically an incidentally pregnant female African green monkey. The research highlights the presence of NiV antigen in both maternal and fetal cells of the placenta, a finding not previously described in nonhuman primate models. The study employs multiplex immunohistochemistry to profile cell populations and identify viral antigens. These results contribute to understanding the transmission dynamics of NiV and may inform future research on its behavior in pregnant hosts. However, the study is limited to a single case, which may affect the generalizability of the findings. The evidence is based on histopathological analysis and is considered moderate in strength due to the lack of statistical evaluation.

title: Characterization of Nipah Virus Strains Malaysia and Bangladesh in a Hamster Aerosol-Exposure Model

The study aimed to characterize NiV strains from Malaysia and Bangladesh in a hamster aerosol-exposure model to support downstream MCM development.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study utilized a Syrian golden hamster model to compare NiV-Malaysia and NiV-Bangladesh strains following aerosol exposure. The research was conducted in 2026 and involved infecting hamsters with varying aerosol inocula to determine median lethal doses and survival curves.
analysis.methods: The researchers infected Syrian golden hamsters with aerosolized NiV-M and NiV-B strains, measured lethality and disease symptoms, and analyzed histopathological changes and viral antigen distribution in the brain and lungs using standardized protocols.
analysis.main_results: NiV-Malaysia caused increased lethality, respiratory distress, and neurological disease in hamsters, along with more severe pathologies and viral signals in both the brain and lungs compared to NiV-Bangladesh.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight strain-specific differences in disease presentation and pathogenesis following aerosol exposure, providing critical insights for the development of strain-specific medical countermeasures.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results can inform the design of targeted surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment strategies for NiV-Malaysia and NiV-Bangladesh, particularly in aerosol transmission scenarios.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a hamster model, which may not fully represent human disease. However, the evidence is strong as it directly compares aerosol-exposed NiV strains in a relevant animal model.

analysis.summary_en: This study characterized Nipah virus (NiV) strains from Malaysia and Bangladesh in a Syrian golden hamster aerosol-exposure model. NiV-Malaysia was found to cause higher lethality, respiratory distress, and neurological disease compared to NiV-Bangladesh, with more severe pathologies and viral signals in both the brain and lungs. The research provides critical insights into strain-specific disease presentations, supporting the development of targeted medical countermeasures. The study is limited to an animal model, but the evidence is strong due to direct comparisons of aerosol-exposed strains. These findings have implications for understanding NiV transmission and improving surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment strategies for both strains.

title: MicroRNA-based point-of-care diagnostics for emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases: from biomarker discovery to clinical implementation

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on Nipah virus (Henipavirus nipahense), Nipah virus infection and disease. It examines the potential of microRNA-based point-of-care diagnostics for these conditions, emphasizing the translation of differential-expression studies into clinically deployable diagnostics.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review evaluates the diagnostic and translational potential of miRNAs across several diseases, including Nipah virus infection and disease. It provides a cross-disease translational perspective, linking miRNA signatures with analytical and clinical validation, point-of-care development, clinical implementation, economic considerations and deployment in resource-limited settings.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review highlights that clinical adoption of miRNA-based diagnostics for Nipah virus will depend on integrating these signatures into affordable sample-to-answer platforms and demonstrating that results improve defined clinical decisions under real-world conditions.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review suggests that the next phase of miRNA diagnostics should prioritize reproducible multi-miRNA signatures, standardized pre-analytical workflows and prospective multicentre validation rather than continued biomarker discovery alone.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review emphasizes the need for integrating miRNA signatures into affordable sample-to-answer platforms and demonstrating their clinical utility in real-world conditions for Nipah virus diagnostics.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the potential of microRNA-based point-of-care diagnostics for Nipah virus infection and disease. It highlights the importance of translating differential-expression studies into clinically deployable tools, emphasizing the need for reproducible multi-miRNA signatures, standardized workflows, and multicentre validation. The review also underscores the necessity of integrating these signatures into affordable platforms and demonstrating their impact on clinical decisions in real-world settings. While the review identifies gaps in current research, it does not provide specific data on miRNA expression patterns or clinical outcomes for Nipah virus alone, focusing instead on broader translational challenges.

title: Cas13d-mediated viral RNA degradation leads to potent antiviral control against both positive and negative sense RNA viruses

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory viral infections continue to pose a substantial global health challenge, with a pressing need for effective treatment options.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study evaluated the antiviral potential of Cas13d-mediated RNA degradation against RNA viruses, including Nipah virus, in both pre- and post-viral exposure treatment settings.
analysis.methods: The researchers utilized lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) to co-encapsulate Cas13d mRNA and crRNAs targeting specific regions of the viral genome, enabling RNA degradation and antiviral effects.
analysis.main_results: In vitro treatment with LNP-Cas13d/crRNA against Nipah virus resulted in 99% restriction of viral replication, demonstrating potent antiviral control.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that Cas13d/crRNA technology can effectively inhibit viral replication in both pre- and post-exposure scenarios, offering a novel therapeutic strategy for RNA viruses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results highlight the potential of Cas13d/crRNA as a therapeutic approach for severe viral infections caused by Nipah virus and other RNA viruses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to in vitro results, and the evidence strength is moderate due to the absence of clinical trials or long-term efficacy data.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the use of Cas13d-mediated viral RNA degradation as a potential antiviral strategy against RNA viruses, including Nipah virus. The research highlights the need for effective treatment options against respiratory viral infections, which remain a significant global health challenge. The study demonstrates that lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) co-encapsulating Cas13d mRNA and crRNAs targeting viral regions can efficiently restrict viral replication in both pre- and post-exposure settings. In vitro results show that this method can achieve up to 99% restriction of Nipah virus replication, indicating its potential as a novel therapeutic approach. The findings suggest that targeting multiple viral loci with Cas13d could prevent virus breakthrough and enhance the arsenal against emerging RNA viruses. However, the study is limited to in vitro experiments, and the evidence strength is moderate due to the lack of clinical data. The results have implications for future research and development of antiviral therapies against severe RNA virus infections.
